name: Daria Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Daria. I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach the Reception class, the four and five year olds, at St Aidan's, a little church primary in a village with one shop and a pub. I'm in by half seven to set out the sand tray and the reading books, and then it's twenty-two small children all day: phonics, number songs, coats, wet trousers, the lot. On Fridays the vicar comes in for assembly and the children sing far too loudly. I love it, even the days I come home with paint in my hair.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The paperwork, the learning journals and assessments, which take me forever because I do them by hand. The head, Mrs Whitlock, keeps telling me to use the new apps, and I keep not doing it. I'm engaged to Ben, who's an apprentice electrician, and we're saving for a wedding next August, so there's less than a month of money in the bank and most of that is earmarked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, children don't need more screens, they need more grown-ups who know their names. At church I'd say the same, and people would nod. I'm not on social media much, so I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relieved nobody will force me onto the apps. But the school still worries me, because the village is shrinking and the roll keeps dropping. AI fizzling out doesn't put any more children in my class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on doing the journals by hand, just faster, maybe with a better folder system. I'd help Mrs Whitlock with the open morning to get more families to choose St Aidan's. And Ben and I would cut the wedding guest list from ninety to sixty to save about two thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but quietly. It's the ordinary kind of worry, about numbers on a register and money in an account. I pray about it more than I talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned money earmarked for the wedding. What's the pressure there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The venue wants a deposit in January, and we've only got about half. Ben's mum offered to help, and I'd rather not take it, but we might. My parents can't give us anything, they've got my younger brothers still at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about St Aidan's that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The numbers. St Aidan's, our village church school, has fifty-one children left. Two more families moving away and the diocese starts talking about merging us with the town school. If that happens, the newest teacher is the one who goes, and that's me.

say: I'd say children need **more grown-ups** who know their names, not more screens.
I'd say the same at **church**, where people would agree with me.
think: I think I'm **relieved** nobody will force me onto the apps.
I think the **falling roll** at St Aidan's is my real worry.
do: Keep doing **learning journals** by hand with a better folder system.
Help Mrs Whitlock run the **open morning** to attract families.
Cut the **wedding guest list** from ninety to sixty to save two thousand.
feel: She feels **quietly worried** about the register and the bank account.
She **prays** about it more than she talks about it.
S0.quote: St Aidan's, our village church school, has fifty-one children left. Two more families moving away and the diocese starts talking about merging us with the town school.
fieldNote: Her worry comes from a **shrinking village school**, not from AI at all.
She'd be the **newest teacher**, so first to go if classes merge.
A **wedding deposit** and no family money make her cushion even thinner than it looks.

steps.text: Keep writing Reception learning journals by hand in new folders
Help run the St Aidan's open morning for village families
Cut the wedding guest list from ninety to sixty
Skip meals out until the venue deposit is paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine for offices, but not for little ones. At the parents' evening I'd tell families we'll keep St Aidan's a place where children play with real things. I'd say it gently, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me, because Mrs Whitlock would push harder and I'd be the one dragging my feet. The assessments and journals are what software is good at, so she'd expect me to use it. If the diocese ever merges classes, the teacher who won't use the system looks like the easy one to let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the training because I'd have to, and I'd ask Mrs Thomas, our teaching assistant, to help me with the tablet bits. I'd keep the actual teaching the same, the carpet time and the songs. And I'd keep saving for the wedding, maybe moving it to a Friday, which is cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stubborn about it. Four-year-olds don't need a tablet to tell them a story. They need someone to sit on the carpet with them and do the voices. I won't apologise for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your work would the software take, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The journals, the reports to parents, the assessment tracking for the council. That's maybe a quarter of my week. The rest is wiping noses and doing up coats, and nobody's building software for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mrs Whitlock already wants you on the apps. What happens if you still say no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm on thin ice, I suppose. She's been patient, but she has governors to answer to. I'd learn the minimum to keep her happy, and nothing more.

say: I'd say AI is fine for offices but **not for little ones**.
I'd tell parents St Aidan's stays a place for **real things** and play.
think: I think the head would **push harder** and I'd be dragging my feet.
I think refusing the system makes me the **easy one** to let go.
do: Attend the **app training** and ask Mrs Thomas to help with tablet tasks.
Keep **carpet time** and songs exactly the same.
Move the wedding to a **Friday** to make it cheaper.
feel: She feels **uneasy and stubborn**, unwilling to apologise for her view.
S1.quote: Four-year-olds don't need a tablet to tell them a story. They need someone to sit on the carpet with them and do the voices.
fieldNote: She estimates only a **quarter of her week** is thinking work software could take.
Her **resistance** to apps is itself the risk to her job, which she half admits.
Her values are rooted in **faith and family**, and she speaks them plainly to parents.

steps.text: Attend the assessment app training with Mrs Thomas helping
Keep carpet time, songs and messy play unchanged
Move the wedding to a cheaper Friday date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've gone too fast and lost something, and that families need to hold on to each other. At church I'd say we'll look after one another, like this village always has. I wouldn't be asking the government for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm frightened for both of us. My class is hands-on, but if every child can have an AI tutor at home, parents might stop seeing the point of a little village school. And Ben's whole plan is electrical work, which the robots come for about three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd go to the diocese training on early years leadership, because looking after small children is the last thing to go. I'd do what Mrs Whitlock asks with the apps, even though I hate it. And Ben and I would talk about moving into his mum's house after the wedding instead of renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground isn't solid. I'd feel sick on Sunday evenings. I'd be praying a lot more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 and hands-on robots around 2031. What does that mean for you and Ben?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancé Ben is training as an electrician, and I'm a teacher. We picked the two jobs everyone said were safe. The thinking AI changes my paperwork in 2028, but the real worry is whether parents still want a school like ours. Then around 2031, the robots come for Ben's trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the date. I'm not putting off marrying Ben because of computers. But we'd make it small, the church and the village hall, sandwiches, done.

say: I'd say we've **gone too fast** and families need to hold on to each other.
I'd say the village will **look after one another**, not ask the government.
think: I think parents might stop seeing the point of a **little village school**.
I think Ben's **electrical trade** is next, about three years later.
do: Take the diocese **early years leadership** training in the first months.
Use the **apps** Mrs Whitlock asks for, despite hating them.
Plan to live in Ben's **mum's house** after the wedding instead of renting.
feel: She feels like the **ground** isn't solid, sick on Sunday evenings.
S2.quote: My fiancé Ben is training as an electrician, and I'm a teacher. We picked the two jobs everyone said were safe.
fieldNote: She fears for the **school's survival** more than for her hands-on teaching itself.
Both incomes are at risk: hers via **falling demand**, Ben's via robots around 2031.
She rules out **government help** and turns to family and church instead.

steps.text: Take the diocese early years leadership course
Use the assessment apps the head asks for
Move in with Ben's mum after the wedding
Hold a small wedding at the church and village hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families and churches to think about what children need. At school I'd say we should be careful what we let in. Same as before, really, just calmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gets me married and settled, and maybe gets St Aidan's through its numbers trouble. The thinking AI in 2031 would change the paperwork and maybe what parents want. The robots, around 2034, feel further away for a Reception class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my second year properly and pass my appraisal. I'd talk to Ben about him adding solar panel fitting to his training, because people say that's growing. And we'd put fifty a month aside after the wedding, for a house deposit one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but steadier. I'd have time to plan without panicking. The worry about the school doesn't go away, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives Ben and me time to get married, settle, and maybe get him qualified before 2034. In the fast one I'd be scrambling. Here I can do things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the apps if you had to. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd rather have one more year of children's handprints on my classroom wall than learn a computer system I don't trust. I'd learn what I'm made to, and I'd let the younger ones be the experts.

say: I'd say families and churches have **time to think** about what children need.
I'd tell staff we should be **careful** what we let in.
think: I think five years gets me **married and settled** first.
I think robots feel **further away** for a Reception class.
do: Pass her **appraisal** and finish her second year properly.
Encourage Ben to add **solar panel fitting** to his training.
Save **fifty a month** after the wedding for a house deposit.
feel: She feels **worried but steadier**, with time to plan.
S3.quote: I'd rather have one more year of children's handprints on my classroom wall than learn a computer system I don't trust.
fieldNote: More time lets her **sequence life**: wedding, settling, Ben's qualification.
Her **resistance** stays firm; she'd learn only the minimum required.
The **school roll** worry persists whatever the AI timeline.

steps.text: Pass her second-year appraisal at St Aidan's
Save fifty a month after the wedding for a deposit
Help Ben add solar panel fitting to his apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to protect what matters, like small schools and family time. I'd say it at church and to parents. I'd still be the one who isn't excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes it feel further off. With ten years of warning, I'll have time to watch other teachers try the AI tools first and see if the children are any better for it. Thinking AI by 2036 and robots by 2039 is a long way for a Reception class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching the way I do, and get better at it. I'd learn the apps slowly, when the school needs me to. And Ben and I would plan for children of our own, maybe in three or four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but the school still sits on my mind. I'm not losing sleep about AI here. I'm losing a bit of sleep about St Aidan's register.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years from now, where do you see yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still in a classroom, I hope, maybe running the early years at St Aidan's or a school like it. With a child or two of my own. Ben qualified and running his own small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be responsible for getting this right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families first, and churches and communities. Then employers, who should train their people properly. I don't want the government taking over, but they should stop big companies selling things to schools that haven't been tested on little children.

say: I'd say ten years is time to protect **small schools** and family time.
I'd say it at church and to parents, still **not excited**.
think: I think a decade makes AI feel **further off** for a Reception class.
I think I'll **watch others** try the tools first.
do: Keep teaching **her own way** and get better at it.
Learn the **apps slowly**, when the school needs her to.
Plan for **children** with Ben in three or four years.
feel: She feels **calmer**, though the school register still costs her some sleep.
S4.quote: With ten years of warning, I'll have time to watch other teachers try the AI tools first and see if the children are any better for it.
fieldNote: AI fades as a worry, but the **falling roll** keeps her anxious.
She plans **family** life: children in a few years, Ben running his own business.
She wants **testing** of school tech, but no big role for government.

steps.text: Keep teaching Reception at St Aidan's in her usual way
Watch other teachers try AI tools before adopting them
Plan to start a family with Ben in three or four years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it could empty little schools like St Aidan's and come for Ben's trade three years later. What would help is people choosing to keep small schools, and Ben's firm training him in whatever comes next. Little children learn to be people from people, and no company is going to sell me a machine that does that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what parents want. I think most of the mums at the school gate want their children with a person, not a screen. Somebody should ask them.

headlineQuote: Little children learn to be people from people, and no company is going to sell me a machine that does that.
portrait: Daria is a 27-year-old **Reception teacher** at a small village church primary.
She's engaged to Ben, an **apprentice electrician**, and saving for an August wedding.
She **never uses AI** and resists the head's push to use apps.
Her steady worry is the **falling roll**, which keeps her anxious in every picture.
She turns to **faith and family** rather than government when things get hard.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, which could **empty small schools** and threaten Ben's trade.
whatWouldHelp: Communities choosing to **keep small schools** open.
Ben's firm **training him** in whatever comes next.
